title: The Unquiet Ledger
premise: Estate lawyer Orsen Brightwater is hired to probate a will for Maren Voss, a woman who vanished seven years ago—and the will's notarization date falls three years after her disappearance. Reading Maren's recovered diary, Orsen finds entries continuing past the date she vanished, suggesting she lived in hiding, watching someone. As Orsen traces the diary's coded references through the town's founding families, she realizes the killer has been feeding her curated evidence, using her reputation for discretion to launder the truth. In the end, Orsen stages a false reading of the estate to force the killer—Maren's own guardian, who faked her death to steal her inheritance—to confess on record, and gives Maren, alive and hidden, the found family she never had.
about_author: Jude Crane spent a decade as a paralegal in small-town probate courts before turning to fiction, and their mysteries are known for legal procedural texture and quietly ferocious protagonists. They live in a converted courthouse with two cats named after dismissed verdicts.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Orsen Brightwater, POV. A courier delivers a sealed will for Maren Voss, missing seven years, notarized four years after her disappearance. Orsen, who prides herself on closable cases, almost refuses—until she notices the notary stamp belongs to a firm that burned down in between. Emotional beat: professional pride curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Inventory of Absence
chapters.summary: Orsen visits Maren's sealed house to catalog the estate. Dust lies undisturbed except on one desk drawer, recently opened. Inside: a diary whose final dated entry is three years after the vanishing. Beat: the thrill of an anomaly—the first crack in a case everyone else closed.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Orsen reads the diary at night, alone. The early entries are ordinary; the later ones are watchful, coded, naming no one but describing being followed by 'the man who counts.' Beat: dread blooming into obsession as Orsen realizes Maren knew she'd disappear.

chapters.title: The Client Who Hired Me
chapters.summary: Orsen tracks the retainer payment to a shell trust administered by Halvard Finch, Maren's former legal guardian and the town's most respected philanthropist. Finch is charming, helpful, and knows details of the case file he shouldn't. Beat: polite menace beneath civility.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Orsen's mentor, retired detective Ada Quill, warns her: the murder statute expires in ninety days, and the original investigators were steered wrong from day one. Someone shaped the file. Beat: stakes crystallized—a ticking clock and a corrupted record.

chapters.title: What the River Kept
chapters.summary: Orsen walks the riverbank where Maren's coat was found, interviewing the fisherman who discovered it. His account contradicts the police report in one crucial detail: the coat was dry. Beat: first hard proof the scene was staged.

chapters.title: The Counting Man
chapters.summary: Decoding the diary's number sequences, Orsen discovers they reference ledger pages from the family shipping business Finch now controls. Maren was auditing him before she vanished. Beat: motive surfaces—inheritance, embezzlement, and a witness who wouldn't stop counting.

chapters.title: Found Family, Borrowed Office
chapters.summary: Orsen's makeshift team coheres: Ada, the fisherman's granddaughter Tally (a records clerk), and Orsen's estranged brother Pell, a forensic accountant. Over takeout in the office, they become something like family. Beat: warmth earned against the cold case.

chapters.title: A Gift of Evidence
chapters.summary: An anonymous package arrives: photographs of the ledger pages Maren referenced. The photos are too perfect—taken from angles only the current custodian could access. Someone is feeding Orsen the case. Beat: paranoia; the helper may be the hunter.

chapters.title: Finch's Version
chapters.summary: Orsen interviews Finch formally. He narrates Maren's history fluently—but repeats a detail from the diary's unpublished later pages verbatim. Orsen says nothing, thanks him, and shakes leaving. Beat: quiet horror masked as a successful interview.

chapters.title: Tally's Discovery
chapters.summary: Tally finds a second notarization under the burned firm's stamp—Maren's own signature, dated after the vanishing. Maren signed documents while officially dead. Beat: hope inverted; Maren lived, which means someone wanted her erased twice.

chapters.title: The House Remembers
chapters.summary: Orsen returns to Maren's house and finds fresh footprints in the cellar dust and a listening device wired into the wall. She leaves it running and speaks aloud, feeding the watcher a false theory. Beat: Orsen seizes agency—turning surveillance into bait.

chapters.title: Pell Runs the Numbers
chapters.summary: Pell reconstructs the ledgers: Finch siphoned Maren's inheritance for years, and the 'missing' Maren had been quietly documenting it. The math is damning but circumstantial. Beat: frustration—the truth is provable only if Finch speaks it himself.

chapters.title: Night Visitor
chapters.summary: Someone enters Orsen's office after hours. Nothing is stolen; instead, the diary is rearranged, its last page torn out. Ada's old instincts read the intrusion as a message: I can reach anything you touch. Beat: violation and fear, the case turning personal.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Orsen reconstructs the torn entry from indentations: a date, a place—the ferry terminal—and the words 'he knows I know.' The statute clock drops below thirty days. Beat: desperation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Trap Design
chapters.summary: The team designs the endgame: a public preliminary reading of the estate where Orsen will present a forged ledger 'proving' Finch innocent, forcing him to correct the record—and confess—in front of witnesses and a court recorder. Beat: tense camaraderie; the plan is elegant and dangerous.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: They rehearse the trap, war-gaming Finch's counters. Ada warns that a man who edits reality will simply deny everything unless cornered absolutely. Orsen adds a final hook: evidence that Maren is alive, which Finch must publicly refute or flee. Beat: nerves braided with loyalty.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Climax begins. At the packed reading, Orsen presents the doctored ledger. Finch, unable to resist correcting the record, dismantles his own alibi piece by piece—until Orsen produces the ferry-terminal ticket stub bearing Maren's post-disappearance signature. Beat: controlled detonation.

chapters.title: Confession on Record
chapters.summary: Cornered by the recorder, the ledger trail, and the living signature, Finch unravels—he admits he staged the drowning and hunted Maren for years. Deputies, tipped by Ada, take him into custody as the statute window closes with hours to spare. Beat: catharsis; the unquiet ledger finally balances.

chapters.title: The Woman Behind the Door
chapters.summary: Following the diary's final coded instruction, Orsen travels to a coastal cottage and meets Maren Voss—alive, wary, seven years ghost. Maren chose invisibility to survive; Orsen offers her something else: names, allies, a table to sit at. Beat: tenderness after tension.

chapters.title: Probate
chapters.summary: Maren, legally resurrected, claims her estate and signs the will that started everything—amending it to leave the house to the fisherman's family and a fund for missing-persons casework bearing Orsen's name. Beat: restoration; power redirected instead of corrupted.

chapters.title: Closing the File
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV, files the final paperwork and keeps one thing unofficial: Sunday dinners with Ada, Tally, Pell—and now Maren. The case that couldn't be closed taught her why she opens doors at all. Beat: quiet resolution; memory honored, family chosen.
